biblical_def: Webster (1828) defines currency first as “Literally, flowing, running or passing.” Of money it is “A continual passing from hand to hand, as coin or bills of credit; circulation” and “That which is current or in circulation, as a medium of trade.” Scripture’s first sale of land is paid in weighed silver, “current money with the merchant” (Gen 23:16). God requires that money be honest: “A false balance is abomination to the LORD: but a just weight is his delight” (Pro 11:1).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): CURRENCY, a flowing or passing; circulation from hand to hand, as coin or bills of credit; that which is current as a medium of trade.
webster_full: CURRENCY, noun [See Current.]
1. Literally, flowing, running or passing; a continued or uninterrupted course, like that of a stream; as the currency of time.
3. A continual passing from hand to hand, as coin or bills of credit; circulation; as the currency of cents, or of English crowns; the currency of bank bills or treasury notes.
4. Fluency; readiness of utterance; but in this sense we generally use fluency.
5. General estimation; the rate at which any thing is generally valued.
He takes greatness of kingdoms according to their bulk and currency and not after intrinsic value.

6. That which is current or in circulation, as a medium of trade. The word may be applied to coins, or to bills issued by authority. It is often applied to bank notes, and to notes issued by government.
scriptures: And Abraham hearkened unto Ephron; and Abraham weighed to Ephron the silver, which he had named in the audience of the sons of Heth, four hundred shekels of silver, current money with the merchant.
A false balance is abomination to the LORD: but a just weight is his delight.
Thy silver is become dross, thy wine mixed with water:
Shew me the tribute money. And they brought unto him a penny.
They say unto him, Caesar's. Then saith he unto them, Render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar's; and unto God the things that are God's.
corruption_summary: Currency is a promise of value passed from hand to hand; debasing it is a false balance.
corruption_paragraphs: Webster ties currency to “General estimation; the rate at which any thing is generally valued.” Money passes only while men trust the measure.

Isaiah charged Jerusalem, “Thy silver is become dross” (Isa 1:22). Christ took the coin that bore Caesar’s image and said, “Render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar’s; and unto God the things that are God’s” (Mat 22:21).
roots_summary: Current: flowing, passing from hand to hand.
roots_lines: Webster (1828): literally, flowing, running or passing.
Webster: that which is current or in circulation, as a medium of trade.
Current money with the merchant (Gen 23:16).
usage: The currency of bank bills or treasury notes

pos: n. & v. (concern; share; premium paid for the use of money)
biblical_def: Webster (1828) defines interest as “Concern; advantage; good”, as “Share; portion; part; participation in value”, and in money matters as “Premium paid for the use of money; the profit per cent derived from money lent.” He adds, “A higher rate of interest than that which the law allows, is called usury.” Webster’s own example of the verb is doctrinal: “Christ, by his atonement, has interested believers in the blessings of the covenant of grace.” The law forbade charging the poor brother: “If thou lend money to any of my people that is poor by thee, thou shalt not be to him as an usurer” (Exo 22:25).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): INTEREST, v. to concern; to give a share in; n. concern; advantage; share; premium paid for the use of money; above the lawful rate it is usury.
webster_full: IN'TEREST, verb transitive [Latin inter and esse.]

1. To concern; to affect; to excite emotion or passion, usually in favor, but sometimes against a person or thing. A narration of suffering interests us in favor of the sufferer. We are interested in the story or in the fate of the sufferer. We are interested to know the result, issue or event of an enterprise. It is followed by in or for. We are interested in the narration, but for the sufferer.
2. To give a share in. Christ, by his atonement, has interested believers in the blessings of the covenant of grace.
3. To have a share.
We are not all interested in the public funds, but we are all interested in the happiness of a free government.
4. To engage; as, to interest one in our favor.
To interest one's self, is to take a share or concern in.
IN'TEREST, noun Concern; advantage; good; as private interest; public interest
Divisions hinder the common interest and public good.
1. Influence over others. They had now lost their interest at court.
He knew his interest sufficient to procure the office.
2. Share; portion; part; participation in value. He has parted with his interest in the stocks. He has an interest in a manufactory of cotton goods.
3. Regard to private profit.
'Tis interest calls off all her sneaking train.

4. Premium paid for the use of money; the profit per cent derived from money lent, or property used by another person, or from debts remaining unpaid. Commercial states have a legal rate of interest Debts on book bear an interest after the expiration of the credit. Courts allow interest in many cases where it is not stipulated. A higher rate of interest than that which the law allows, is called usury.
Simple interest is that which arises from the principal sum only.
Compound interest is that which arises from the principal with the interest added; interest on interest
5. Any surplus advantage.
With all speed,
you shall have your desire with interest
scriptures: If thou lend money to any of my people that is poor by thee, thou shalt not be to him as an usurer, neither shalt thou lay upon him usury.
Thou shalt not lend upon usury to thy brother; usury of money, usury of victuals, usury of any thing that is lent upon usury:
He that putteth not out his money to usury, nor taketh reward against the innocent. He that doeth these things shall never be moved.
Thou oughtest therefore to have put my money to the exchangers, and then at my coming I should have received mine own with usury.
corruption_summary: Interest on money is lawful in Webster’s day and in Christ’s parable; profit taken from a poor brother’s need is not.
corruption_paragraphs: In the parable the lord tells the idle servant he should have put the money “to the exchangers” (Mat 25:27). Scripture’s prohibition falls on lending to a brother in need (Exo 22:25; Deu 23:19).
The man who dwells in God’s tabernacle “putteth not out his money to usury” (Psa 15:5). Webster draws the line at the lawful rate.
roots_summary: Latin inter esse: to be between; a share in a thing.
roots_lines: Webster (1828): concern; advantage; good.
Webster: premium paid for the use of money.
Neither shalt thou lay upon him usury (Exo 22:25).

pos: n. (the sole power of selling a kind of goods)
biblical_def: Webster (1828) defines a monopoly as “The sole power of vending any species of goods, obtained either by engrossing the articles in market by purchase, or by a license from the government confirming this privilege.” He adds that “Monopolies by individuals obtained by engrossing, are an offense prohibited by law.” Scripture condemns the engrosser of grain: “He that withholdeth corn, the people shall curse him: but blessing shall be upon the head of him that selleth it” (Pro 11:26). The Philistines kept a monopoly of the smith’s craft: “there was no smith found throughout all the land of Israel” (1Sa 13:19).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): MONOPOLY, the sole power of vending any species of goods, by engrossing the market or by government license.
webster_full: MONOP'OLY, noun [Latin monopolium.] The sole power of vending any species of goods, obtained either by engrossing the articles in market by purchase, or by a license from the government confirming this privilege. Thus the East India Company in Great Britain has a monopoly of the trade to the East Indies, granted to them by charter. Monopolies by individuals obtained by engrossing, are an offense prohibited by law. But a man has by natural right the exclusive power of vending his own produce or manufactures, and to retain that exclusive right is not a monopoly within the meaning of law.
scriptures: He that withholdeth corn, the people shall curse him: but blessing shall be upon the head of him that selleth it.
Woe unto them that join house to house, that lay field to field, till there be no place, that they may be placed alone in the midst of the earth!
Now there was no smith found throughout all the land of Israel: for the Philistines said, Lest the Hebrews make them swords or spears:
But all the Israelites went down to the Philistines, to sharpen every man his share, and his coulter, and his axe, and his mattock.
corruption_summary: A monopoly gained by engrossing withholds bread from the people; Webster distinguishes it from a man’s right to sell his own work.
corruption_paragraphs: Webster says “a man has by natural right the exclusive power of vending his own produce or manufactures.” That is not a monopoly in law.
The prophet pronounced woe on those who “join house to house, that lay field to field, till there be no place” (Isa 5:8).
roots_lines: Webster (1828): the sole power of vending any species of goods.
He that withholdeth corn, the people shall curse him (Pro 11:26).

pos: n. (a fixed yearly recompense for service)
etymology: Webster (1828): [Latin salarium; said to be from sal, salt, which was part of the pay of Roman soldiers.]
biblical_def: Webster (1828) defines a salary as “The recompense or consideration stipulated to be paid to a person for services, usually a fixed sum to be paid by the year.” He distinguishes it from wages: “When wages are stated or stipulated by the month, week or day, we do not call the compensation salary but pay or wages.” Christ sets the principle: “the labourer is worthy of his hire” (Luk 10:7). Paul applies it to those who labour in the word (1Ti 5:18).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): SALARY, the recompense stipulated to be paid for services, usually a fixed sum by the year.
webster_full: SAL'ARY, noun [Latin salarium; said to be from sal, salt, which was part of the pay of Roman soldiers.]

The recompense or consideration stipulated to be paid to a person for services, usually a fixed sum to be paid by the year, as to governors, magistrates, settled clergymen, instructors of seminaries, or other officers, civil or ecclesiastical. When wages are stated or stipulated by the month, week or day, we do not call the compensation salary but pay or wages; as in the case of military men and laborers.
scriptures: And in the same house remain, eating and drinking such things as they give: for the labourer is worthy of his hire. Go not from house to house.
For the scripture saith, Thou shalt not muzzle the ox that treadeth out the corn. And, The labourer is worthy of his reward.
And the soldiers likewise demanded of him, saying, And what shall we do? And he said unto them, Do violence to no man, neither accuse any falsely; and be content with your wages.

Behold, the hire of the labourers who have reaped down your fields, which is of you kept back by fraud, crieth: and the cries of them which have reaped are entered into the ears of the Lord of sabaoth.
corruption_summary: A salary is a promise to pay; keeping it back is fraud before the Lord of sabaoth.
corruption_paragraphs: Webster names those who receive salaries: “governors, magistrates, settled clergymen, instructors of seminaries, or other officers, civil or ecclesiastical.”
John told soldiers, “be content with your wages” (Luk 3:14). James warns that pay “kept back by fraud, crieth” (Jas 5:4).
roots_summary: Latin salarium, said by Webster to come from sal, salt.
roots_lines: Webster (1828): the recompense or consideration stipulated to be paid to a person for services.
The labourer is worthy of his hire (Luk 10:7).
usage: A fixed sum to be paid by the year

pos: n. (a bag and its contents; a stock; a statement of finances)
biblical_def: Webster (1828) defines a budget first as “A bag; a little sack, with its contents. Hence, a stock or store.” In government it is “The papers respecting the finances of the British nation.” To open the budget is “to lay before a legislative body the papers of the Executive Government.” Christ assumes that a builder counts before he builds: “which of you, intending to build a tower, sitteth not down first, and counteth the cost, whether he have sufficient to finish it?” (Luk 14:28).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): BUDGET, a bag with its contents; a stock or store; the papers respecting the finances of the nation.
webster_full: BUDG'ET, noun
1. A bag; a little sack, with its contents. Hence, a stock or store; as a budget of inventions.
2. The papers respecting the finances of the British nation.
To open the budget to lay before a legislative body the papers of the Executive Government.
scriptures: For which of you, intending to build a tower, sitteth not down first, and counteth the cost, whether he have sufficient to finish it?
Be thou diligent to know the state of thy flocks, and look well to thy herds.
There is treasure to be desired and oil in the dwelling of the wise; but a foolish man spendeth it up.
corruption_summary: A budget is a counting of the cost before the spending; Scripture calls that wisdom.
corruption_paragraphs: Webster’s budget began as a bag and its contents: what a man actually holds.
“There is treasure to be desired and oil in the dwelling of the wise; but a foolish man spendeth it up” (Pro 21:20). The steward must “know the state of thy flocks” (Pro 27:23).
roots_summary: A bag, then the stock it holds, then a nation’s accounts.
roots_lines: Webster (1828): a bag; a little sack, with its contents.
Webster: the papers respecting the finances of the British nation.
Counteth the cost (Luk 14:28).

pos: n. & v. (an inland duty on goods consumed)
etymology: Webster (1828): [Latin excisum, cut off, from excido.]
biblical_def: Webster (1828) defines an excise as “An inland duty or impost, laid on commodities consumed, or on the retail, which is the last state before consumption.” As a verb it means “To lay or impose a duty on articles consumed.” Scripture names the ancient forms of the same burden, “toll, tribute, and custom” (Ezr 4:13), and commands the Christian to pay: “Render therefore to all their dues: tribute to whom tribute is due; custom to whom custom” (Rom 13:7).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): EXCISE, an inland duty or impost laid on commodities consumed or on the retail; v. to lay such a duty.
webster_full: EXCI'SE, noun s as z. [Latin excisum, cut off, from excido.]

An inland duty or impost, laid on commodities consumed, or on the retail, which is the last state before consumption; as an excise on coffee, soap, candles, which a person consumes in his family. But many articles are excised at the manufactories, as spirit at the distillery, printed silks and linens at the printer's, etc.
EXCI'SE, verb transitive s as z. To lay or impose a duty on articles consumed, or in the hands of merchants, manufacturers and retailers; to levy an excise on.
scriptures: Render therefore to all their dues: tribute to whom tribute is due; custom to whom custom; fear to whom fear; honour to whom honour.
Be it known now unto the king, that, if this city be builded, and the walls set up again, then will they not pay toll, tribute, and custom, and so thou shalt endamage the revenue of the kings.

Also we certify you, that touching any of the priests and Levites, singers, porters, Nethinims, or ministers of this house of God, it shall not be lawful to impose toll, tribute, or custom, upon them.

He saith, Yes. And when he was come into the house, Jesus prevented him, saying, What thinkest thou, Simon? of whom do the kings of the earth take custom or tribute? of their own children, or of strangers?
corruption_summary: An excise is a lawful due when lawfully laid; Scripture also records rulers who exempted God’s servants from such dues.
corruption_paragraphs: Webster’s examples are household goods: “an excise on coffee, soap, candles, which a person consumes in his family.”

Artaxerxes decreed that on the priests and Levites “it shall not be lawful to impose toll, tribute, or custom” (Ezr 7:24). Christ asked of whom “the kings of the earth take custom or tribute” (Mat 17:25).
roots_lines: Webster (1828): an inland duty or impost.
Custom to whom custom (Rom 13:7).
usage: An excise on coffee, soap, candles

pos: n. (one who seeks or is proposed for an office)
biblical_def: Webster (1828) defines a candidate as “A man who seeks or aspires to an office; one who offers himself” for preferment, “as a candidate for the office of sheriff.” He also gives a church sense, “A man who is qualified, according to the rules of the church, to preach the gospel”, and a final one: “One who is in a state of trial or probation for a reward, in another life; as a candidate for heaven or for eternity.” Scripture tests candidates before office: “let these also first be proved; then let them use the office of a deacon, being found blameless” (1Ti 3:10).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): CANDIDATE, one who seeks or aspires to an office; one proposed for preferment; one qualified to preach; one in probation for a reward in another life.
webster_full: CANDIDATE, noun
1. A man who seeks or aspires to an office; one who offers himself,
usually followed by for; as a candidate for the office of sheriff.
2. One who is in contemplation for an office, or for preferment, by those who have power to elect or appoint, though he does not offer himself.
3. One who, by his services or actions, will or may justly obtain preferment or reward, or whose conduct tends to secure it; as a candidate for praise.
4. A man who is qualified, according to the rules of the church, to preach the gospel, and take the charge of a parish or religious society, and proposes to settle in the ministry.
5. One who is in a state of trial or probation for a reward, in another life; as a candidate for heaven or for eternity.
scriptures: And let these also first be proved; then let them use the office of a deacon, being found blameless.
Wherefore, brethren, look ye out among you seven men of honest report, full of the Holy Ghost and wisdom, whom we may appoint over this business.
Take you wise men, and understanding, and known among your tribes, and I will make them rulers over you.
Wherefore now let the fear of the LORD be upon you; take heed and do it: for there is no iniquity with the LORD our God, nor respect of persons, nor taking of gifts.
corruption_summary: A candidate is to be proved before he is trusted; Scripture asks first for honest report and the fear of God.
corruption_paragraphs: The church chose men “of honest report, full of the Holy Ghost and wisdom” (Act 6:3). Israel was told to take “wise men, and understanding, and known among your tribes” (Deu 1:13).
Webster’s last sense reminds every candidate that a greater election is pending: “a candidate for heaven or for eternity.”
roots_summary: One who seeks or is proposed for an office.
roots_lines: Webster (1828): a man who seeks or aspires to an office.
Let these also first be proved (1Ti 3:10).
usage: A candidate for the office of sheriff

pos: n. (a meeting; the legislature of the United States)
etymology: Webster (1828): [Latin , to come together; to go or step; a step. See Grade and Degree.]
biblical_def: Webster (1828) defines a congress first as “A meeting of individuals; an assembly of envoys, commissioners, deputies, etc.” In America it is “the legislature of the United States, consisting of two houses, a senate and a house of representatives.” Scripture records councils that met to judge a question: “the apostles and elders came together for to consider of this matter” (Act 15:6), and their letter began, “it seemed good to the Holy Ghost, and to us” (Act 15:28).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): CONGRESS, a meeting of individuals; an assembly of envoys or deputies; the legislature of the United States, a senate and a house of representatives.
webster_full: CONGRESS, noun [Latin , to come together; to go or step; a step. See Grade and Degree.]

1. A meeting of individuals; an assembly of envoys, commissioners, deputies, etc., particularly a meeting of the representatives of several courts, to concert measures for their common good, or to adjust their mutual concerns.
2. The assembly of delegates of the several British Colonies in America, which united to resist the claims of Great Britain in 1774, and which declared the colonies independent.

3. The assembly of the delegates of the several United States, after the declaration of Independence, and until the adoption of the present constitution, and the organization of the government in 1789. During these periods, the congress consisted of one house only.

4. The assembly of senators and representatives of the several states of North America, according to the present constitution, or political compact, by which they are united in a federal republic; the legislature of the United States, consisting of two houses, a senate and a house of representatives. Members of the senate are elected for six years, but the members of the house of representatives are chosen for two years only. Hence the united body of senators and representatives for the two years , during which the representatives hold their seats is called one congress Thus we say the first or second session of the sixteenth congress
5. A meeting of two or more persons in a contest; an encounter; a conflict.
6. The meeting of the sexes in sexual commerce.
scriptures: And the apostles and elders came together for to consider of this matter.
For it seemed good to the Holy Ghost, and to us, to lay upon you no greater burden than these necessary things;

Then Solomon assembled the elders of Israel, and all the heads of the tribes, the chief of the fathers of the children of Israel, unto king Solomon in Jerusalem, that they might bring up the ark of the covenant of the LORD out of the city of David, which is Zion.
Judges and officers shalt thou make thee in all thy gates, which the LORD thy God giveth thee, throughout thy tribes: and they shall judge the people with just judgment.
corruption_summary: Webster records the American Congress as delegates who first met to resist and then to govern; every legislature sits under God’s law.
corruption_paragraphs: Webster’s second sense is the assembly “which united to resist the claims of Great Britain in 1774, and which declared the colonies independent.”
Israel’s assemblies gathered “the elders of Israel, and all the heads of the tribes” (1Ki 8:1). Judges were to “judge the people with just judgment” (Deu 16:18).
roots_summary: Latin, to come together: a meeting, then a nation’s legislature.
roots_lines: Webster (1828): a meeting of individuals.
Webster: the legislature of the United States.
The apostles and elders came together (Act 15:6).

pos: n. (a proclamation of command by authority)
etymology: Webster (1828): [Latin edictum, from edico, to utter or proclaim; e and dico, to speak.]
biblical_def: Webster (1828) defines an edict as “That which is uttered or proclaimed by authority as a rule of action; an order issued by a prince to his subjects, as a rule or law requiring obedience.” Scripture records edicts that bound the conscience against God. Darius signed the writing “according to the law of the Medes and Persians, which altereth not” (Dan 6:8), and Daniel kept praying (Dan 6:10). The apostles answered every such command: “We ought to obey God rather than men” (Act 5:29).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): EDICT, that which is proclaimed by authority as a rule of action; an order of a prince to his subjects requiring obedience.
webster_full: E'DICT, noun [Latin edictum, from edico, to utter or proclaim; e and dico, to speak.]

That which is uttered or proclaimed by authority as a rule of action; an order issued by a prince to his subjects, as a rule or law requiring obedience; a proclamation of command or prohibition. An edict is an order or ordinance of a sovereign prince, intended as a permanent law, or to erect a new office, to establish new duties, or other temporary regulation; as the edicts of the Roman emperors; the edicts of the French monarch.
scriptures: Now, O king, establish the decree, and sign the writing, that it be not changed, according to the law of the Medes and Persians, which altereth not.
Then Peter and the other apostles answered and said, We ought to obey God rather than men.
But the midwives feared God, and did not as the king of Egypt commanded them, but saved the men children alive.
By faith Moses, when he was born, was hid three months of his parents, because they saw he was a proper child; and they were not afraid of the king's commandment.

Write ye also for the Jews, as it liketh you, in the king's name, and seal it with the king's ring: for the writing which is written in the king's name, and sealed with the king's ring, may no man reverse.
corruption_summary: An edict binds subjects in lawful things; when it commands sin, God’s word outranks the prince’s.
corruption_paragraphs: The Hebrew midwives “feared God, and did not as the king of Egypt commanded them” (Exo 1:17). Moses’ parents “were not afraid of the king’s commandment” (Heb 11:23).
Esther’s counter-decree shows an edict answered lawfully, under the king’s seal (Est 8:8).
roots_summary: Latin edico: to speak out, to proclaim.
roots_lines: Webster (1828): that which is uttered or proclaimed by authority as a rule of action.
We ought to obey God rather than men (Act 5:29).
usage: The edicts of the Roman emperors
A proclamation of command or prohibition

pos: n. v. & adj. (one sent to act for another)
biblical_def: Webster (1828) defines a delegate as “A person appointed and sent by another with powers to transact business as his representative; a deputy; a commissioner.” In America he is “a person elected or appointed to represent a state or a district, in the Congress, or in a Convention for forming or altering a constitution.” The verb means “To entrust; to commit; to deliver to anothers care and exercise.” Israel sent a man from each tribe, “every one a ruler among them” (Num 13:2), and the churches sent men Paul called “the messengers of the churches, and the glory of Christ” (2Co 8:23).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): DELEGATE, v. to send with power to act; to entrust; n. a person appointed and sent to act as another’s representative; a deputy.
webster_full: DELEGATE, verb transitive [Latin To send.]
1. To send away; appropriately, to send on an embassy; to send with power to transact business, as a representative. The President delegated three commissioners to the court of St. Cloud.
2. To entrust; to commit; to deliver to anothers care and exercise; as, to delegate authority or power to an envoy, representative or judge.
DELEGATE, noun

1. A person appointed and sent by another with powers to transact business as his representative; a deputy; a commissioner; a vicar. In the United States, a person elected or appointed to represent a state or a district, in the Congress, or in a Convention for forming or altering a constitution.

2. In Great Britain, a commissioner appointed by the king, under the great seal, to hear and determine appeals from the ecclesiastical court. Hence the Court of Delegates is the great court of appeal in all ecclesiastical causes. It is used also for the court of appeals from that of the admiralty.
3. A layman appointed to attend an ecclesiastical council.
DELEGATE, adjective Deputed; sent to act for or represent another; as a delegate judge.
scriptures: Send thou men, that they may search the land of Canaan, which I give unto the children of Israel: of every tribe of their fathers shall ye send a man, every one a ruler among them.
Whether any do enquire of Titus, he is my partner and fellowhelper concerning you: or our brethren be enquired of, they are the messengers of the churches, and the glory of Christ.

When therefore Paul and Barnabas had no small dissension and disputation with them, they determined that Paul and Barnabas, and certain other of them, should go up to Jerusalem unto the apostles and elders about this question.

And let them judge the people at all seasons: and it shall be, that every great matter they shall bring unto thee, but every small matter they shall judge: so shall it be easier for thyself, and they shall bear the burden with thee.
corruption_summary: A delegate carries authority that is not his own and must answer to those who sent him.
corruption_paragraphs: Webster’s delegate holds “powers to transact business as his representative.” The power is lent, not owned.
Antioch sent Paul and Barnabas “up to Jerusalem unto the apostles and elders about this question” (Act 15:2). Moses delegated the small matters and kept the great (Exo 18:22).
roots_summary: Latin, to send: one sent with power to act.
roots_lines: Webster (1828): a person appointed and sent by another with powers to transact business as his representative.
Every one a ruler among them (Num 13:2).

pos: n. (one who flees to a place of safety)
biblical_def: Webster (1828) defines a refugee as “One who flies to a shelter or place of safety” and as one who, “in times of persecution or political commotion, flees to a foreign country for safety.” The law appointed “cities of refuge” for the slayer who killed unawares (Num 35:11). The Lord Himself was carried into Egypt as a child when the angel said, “flee into Egypt” (Mat 2:13).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): REFUGEE, one who flies to a shelter or place of safety; one who flees to a foreign country in times of persecution or political commotion.
webster_full: REFUGEE', noun
1. One who flies to a shelter or place of safety.

2. One who, in times of persecution or political commotion, flees to a foreign country for safety; as the French refugees, who left France after the revocation of the edict of Nantz, and settled in Flanders and America; the refugees from Hispaniola, in 1792; and the American refugees, who left their country at the revolution.
scriptures: Then ye shall appoint you cities to be cities of refuge for you; that the slayer may flee thither, which killeth any person at unawares.

And when they were departed, behold, the angel of the Lord appeareth to Joseph in a dream, saying, Arise, and take the young child and his mother, and flee into Egypt, and be thou there until I bring thee word: for Herod will seek the young child to destroy him.
Thou shalt not deliver unto his master the servant which is escaped from his master unto thee:
But the stranger that dwelleth with you shall be unto you as one born among you, and thou shalt love him as thyself; for ye were strangers in the land of Egypt: I am the LORD your God.
That by two immutable things, in which it was impossible for God to lie, we might have a strong consolation, who have fled for refuge to lay hold upon the hope set before us:
corruption_summary: The refugee flees for safety; Scripture ordered shelter under law and reminds Israel that they were strangers too.
corruption_paragraphs: Israel was told not to return the escaped servant: “Thou shalt not deliver unto his master the servant which is escaped from his master unto thee” (Deu 23:15). The stranger was to be loved “for ye were strangers in the land of Egypt” (Lev 19:34).
Believers are refugees of another kind, “who have fled for refuge to lay hold upon the hope set before us” (Heb 6:18).
roots_summary: One who flies to a refuge.

pos: n. (robbery on the sea; the taking of another’s writings)
etymology: Webster (1828): [Latin piratica, from Gr. to attempt, to dare, to enterprise, whence Latin periculum, experior; Eng. to fare.]
biblical_def: Webster (1828) defines piracy as “The act, practice or crime of robbing on the high seas”, “a crime that answers to robbery on land.” His second sense is “The robbing of another by taking his writings.” The eighth commandment covers both: “Thou shalt not steal” (Exo 20:15). The LORD named the literary thief among the prophets: “I am against the prophets, saith the LORD, that steal my words every one from his neighbour” (Jer 23:30).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): PIRACY, robbery on the high seas; the robbing of another by taking his writings.
webster_full: PI'RACY, noun [Latin piratica, from Gr. to attempt, to dare, to enterprise, whence Latin periculum, experior; Eng. to fare.]
1. The act, practice or crime of robbing on the high seas; the taking of property from others by open violence and without authority, on the sea; a crime that answers to robbery on land.
Other acts than robbery on the high seas, are declared by statute to be piracy See Act of Congress, April 30, 1790.
2. The robbing of another by taking his writings.
scriptures: Therefore, behold, I am against the prophets, saith the LORD, that steal my words every one from his neighbour.
Let him that stole steal no more: but rather let him labour, working with his hands the thing which is good, that he may have to give to him that needeth.
corruption_summary: Webster counted taking another man’s writings as piracy; copying is still theft when the work is not yours.
corruption_paragraphs: Webster files the taking of writings under robbery, not under borrowing.
The cure is work: “Let him that stole steal no more: but rather let him labour” (Eph 4:28).
roots_summary: Latin piratica: sea-robbery, then the theft of writings.
